blocks.text: OpenHands Teams brings enterprise AI agent capabilities to engineering teams through self-service, making it easier to build automated engineering workflows on your own infrastructure, starting with vulnerability remediation.

inlines.text: OpenHands Teams brings enterprise AI agent capabilities to engineering teams through self-service, making it easier to build automated engineering workflows on your own infrastructure, starting with vulnerability remediation.

blocks.text: Vulnerability management is becoming increasingly challenging as the number of reported software vulnerabilities continues to grow, with AI-assisted discovery adding to the pressure. Security tools have made it easier to identify vulnerable dependencies and affected applications, but resolving those findings still requires substantial engineering effort. Teams must investigate the impact, determine the appropriate remediation, implement changes, validate the results, and prepare fixes for review. When vulnerabilities affect multiple repositories, that work compounds.

blocks.text: AI coding agents can tackle individual engineering tasks, but much of that work still depends on someone initiating an agent session and coordinating the next steps. The bigger opportunity is connecting agents to the tools and events that drive engineering work, allowing them to investigate issues, implement changes, and validate results through repeatable workflows, with human oversight where needed.

blocks.text: Why vulnerability remediation needs a different approach

inlines.text: Why vulnerability remediation needs a different approach

blocks.text: Organizations already invest in vulnerability scanning, dependency monitoring, and security tooling. These systems help identify potential exposure, but resolving a finding often requires engineers to investigate the affected code, determine the appropriate remediation, implement changes, and validate that the fix doesn’t introduce regressions.

inlines.text: Organizations already invest in vulnerability scanning, dependency monitoring, and security tooling. These systems help identify potential exposure, but resolving a finding often requires engineers to investigate the affected code, determine the appropriate remediation, implement changes, and validate that the fix doesn’t introduce regressions.

blocks.text: That work becomes particularly demanding when a vulnerable dependency appears across multiple repositories or when a patch requires application changes rather than a straightforward version update.

inlines.text: That work becomes particularly demanding when a vulnerable dependency appears across multiple repositories or when a patch requires application changes rather than a straightforward version update.

blocks.text: A typical remediation process involves:

inlines.text: A typical remediation process involves:
Identifying affected repositories and dependencies.
Determining whether vulnerable functionality is actually used.
Selecting a compatible patch or mitigation.
Updating dependencies or application code.
Running tests and investigating failures.
Preparing changes for developer review.

blocks.text: Each step requires engineering time, often pulling developers away from planned work. As new vulnerabilities are discovered, the backlog can grow faster than teams can investigate and resolve findings.

inlines.text: Each step requires engineering time, often pulling developers away from planned work. As new vulnerabilities are discovered, the backlog can grow faster than teams can investigate and resolve findings.

blocks.text: Coding agents can help with much of this work, but using an agent to address each vulnerability individually doesn’t solve the coordination problem. Someone still needs to identify the issue, provide the right context, initiate the task, and review the results.

inlines.text: Coding agents can help with much of this work, but using an agent to address each vulnerability individually doesn’t solve the coordination problem. Someone still needs to identify the issue, provide the right context, initiate the task, and review the results.

blocks.text: By connecting vulnerability findings to repeatable agent workflows, teams can automate much of the investigation, implementation, and validation while retaining human approval over changes.

A software factory connects those capabilities to automated workflows that respond to new findings, carry out remediation work, and involve engineers when decisions or approvals are required.

blocks.text: Traditional automation works well when the steps are predictable. Agent-driven workflows can handle tasks that require investigation and adaptation, such as determining whether a dependency upgrade will introduce breaking changes or diagnosing why a vulnerability still appears in production scans after a fix has merged.

blocks.text: How we patch our own container images

inlines.text: How we patch our own container images

blocks.text: We use OpenHands to automate vulnerability remediation for our own product. A scanner checks our container images, including third-party images we redistribute, and an OpenHands automation acts on the findings. The agent’s instructions read less like a script and more like a job description: you own the security patch backlog, and your job is action, not reporting.

inlines.text: We use OpenHands to automate vulnerability remediation for our own product. A scanner checks our container images, including third-party images we redistribute, and an OpenHands automation acts on the findings. The agent’s instructions read less like a script and more like a job description:
you own the security patch backlog, and your job is action, not reporting.

blocks.text: Each run, the agent:

inlines.text: Each run, the agent:
Identifies and prioritizes vulnerabilities.
It reads the latest scan, focuses on critical and high-severity findings with available fixes, and prioritizes changes based on their impact.
Processes existing dependency updates.
It updates stale Dependabot branches, investigates minor CI failures, and merges low-risk changes that pass CI.
Prepares additional fixes.
It opens pull requests for remaining vulnerabilities, grouping compatible changes by repository and separating major version upgrades with documented breaking changes.
Validates changes.
It runs changes through CI, investigates failures, and revisits unresolved issues in subsequent runs.
Verifies remediation in production.
A merged PR isn’t the finish line. The workflow tracks findings until subsequent scans confirm that the affected CVEs are no longer reported.
Reports progress and escalates decisions.
A Slack summary captures what’s merged, what’s still open, and what requires human review.

blocks.text: Guardrails for autonomous remediation

inlines.text: Guardrails for autonomous remediation

blocks.text: We configure the workflow with explicit rules that limit how the agent operates.

inlines.text: We configure the workflow with explicit rules that limit how the agent operates.
Risk-based changes:
Each PR receives an explained risk score from 1 to 10, with automated merging limited to low-risk changes that pass CI.
Limits on work on progress:
The agent is instructed to make no more than three merges per run and maintain no more than three open PRs.
No vulnerability suppression:
Findings must be resolved through upgrades or rebuilds rather than suppressed.
Restricted access:
The workflow uses a dedicated machine user and prohibits direct pushes to default or release branches.
Respect for developer decisions:
PRs closed without merging are not automatically retried.

blocks.text: The workflow combines agent reasoning with the automations, integrations, and execution environments needed to run remediation repeatedly. OpenHands provides the infrastructure to operate these workflows while giving engineering teams visibility into agent activity and control over execution.

blocks.text: How OpenHands powers automated remediation workflows

inlines.text: How OpenHands powers automated remediation workflows

blocks.text: Getting an agent to investigate and fix a vulnerability in one repository is relatively straightforward. Making that workflow reliable enough to run repeatedly across repositories introduces a different set of challenges. Teams need to determine what triggers the agent, what context it receives, where it executes, how it handles failures, and which changes it can make autonomously versus those requiring human approval. They also need visibility into what agents are doing and controls over what they can access.

Run scheduled and event-driven workflows with built-in integrations for GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Azure DevOps, Jira, and more.
Team management and security:
Manage users and permissions with role-based access controls (RBAC) and single sign-on (SSO).
